[2024 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Part I, Problem 1 (MLE and Hypothesis Testing for Exponential Family). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. from a one-parameter exponential family $p(x \mid \theta) = h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta) T(x) - B(\theta)\}$, with natural form $p(x \mid \eta) = h(x)\exp\{\eta T(x) - A(\eta)\}$ ($\eta$ canonical).
(a) Identify the sufficient statistic for $\theta$ and compute the MLE of $\theta$.
(b) State $A(\eta)$ in terms of $\theta$.
(c) ($\clubsuit$) Assume $T(x)$ is not constant on the support and $\eta(\theta)$ is one-to-one. Show the MLE is unique. (Hint: show $A(\eta)$ is strictly convex.)
(For (d)-(f) assume $\eta(\theta)$ strictly increasing and $\sum_i T(X_i)$ continuous.) (d) Construct the most powerful test for $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta = \theta_1$ with $\theta_1 > \theta_0$.
(e) Construct the UMP test for $H_0 : \theta \le \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta > \theta_0$ and justify why it is UMP.
(f) Prove or disprove the existence of a UMP test for $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$.

Let  
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i),\qquad \bar T_n=S_n/n,
\]
and let \(\mathcal H\) denote the natural parameter space for \(\eta\). The joint density in canonical form is
\[
L(\eta;x_{1:n})
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta S_n-nA(\eta)\}.
\]

---

## (a) Sufficient statistic and MLE

By the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem,
\[
L(\theta;x_{1:n})
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\},
\]
so the statistic
\[
\boxed{S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)}
\]
is sufficient for \(\theta\).

The log-likelihood, up to an additive constant not depending on \(\theta\), is
\[
\ell(\theta)=\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta).
\]

Equivalently, in the canonical parameterization,
\[
\ell(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]

An interior MLE \(\widehat \eta\) satisfies the likelihood equation
\[
0=\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \eta}
=S_n-nA'(\eta),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{A'(\widehat\eta)=\bar T_n.}
\]

Thus, whenever \(\bar T_n\) lies in the range of \(A'\),
\[
\boxed{\widehat\eta=(A')^{-1}(\bar T_n).}
\]

Then the MLE for \(\theta\) is any \(\widehat\theta\) satisfying
\[
\eta(\widehat\theta)=\widehat\eta.
\]
If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then
\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\eta^{-1}\!\left((A')^{-1}(\bar T_n)\right).}
\]

Equivalently, differentiating with respect to \(\theta\),
\[
0=\ell'(\theta)=\eta'(\theta)S_n-nB'(\theta),
\]
so an interior MLE satisfies
\[
\boxed{\frac{B'(\widehat\theta)}{\eta'(\widehat\theta)}=\bar T_n}
\]
when \(\eta'(\widehat\theta)\neq 0\).

Boundary cases may occur if \(\bar T_n\) is outside the range of \(A'\).

---

## (b) Expression for \(A(\eta)\) in terms of \(\theta\)

The canonical log-partition function is
\[
A(\eta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]

Since
\[
p(x\mid \theta)=h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}
\]
is normalized, we must have
\[
B(\theta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta(\theta)T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{B(\theta)=A(\eta(\theta)).}
\]

If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then for \(\eta=\eta(\theta)\),
\[
\boxed{A(\eta)=B(\eta^{-1}(\eta)).}
\]

---

## (c) Uniqueness of the MLE

Assume \(T(x)\) is not constant on the support and \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one.

For \(\eta\in \mathcal H\),
\[
A(\eta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta T(x)}\,d\mu(x).
\]

In a regular exponential family,
\[
A'(\eta)=\mathbb E_\eta[T(X)]
\]
and
\[
A''(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X)).
\]

Because \(T(X)\) is not almost surely constant under \(P_\eta\), we have
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X))>0.
\]
Therefore
\[
A''(\eta)>0,
\]
so \(A\) is strictly convex.

The canonical log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]
Since \(A\) is strictly convex, \(-A\) is strictly concave, and hence \(\ell(\eta)\) is strictly concave in \(\eta\). Therefore \(\ell(\eta)\) has at most one maximizer over the natural parameter space.

Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, a unique maximizer in \(\eta\) corresponds to a unique maximizer in \(\theta\). Thus, whenever the MLE exists,

\[
\boxed{\text{the MLE is unique.}}
\]

---

For parts (d)–(f), fix a significance level \(0<\alpha<1\). Also assume \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(S_n\) has a continuous distribution.

---

## (d) Most powerful test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta=\theta_1\), \(\theta_1>\theta_0\)

Let
\[
\eta_j=\eta(\theta_j),\qquad j=0,1.
\]
Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),
\[
\eta_1>\eta_0.
\]

The likelihood ratio is
\[
\frac{L(\theta_1)}{L(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta_1-\eta_0)S_n-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]\right\}.
\]

Because \(\eta_1-\eta_0>0\), this likelihood ratio is an increasing function of \(S_n\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large values of \(S_n\).

Choose \(c_\alpha\) such that
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]
Because \(S_n\) is continuous, no randomization is needed.

Thus the MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
}
\]

---

## (e) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

Consider the same test
\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\},
}
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

First, we show that this test has level \(\alpha\) for the composite null. For fixed \(c\), define
\[
\beta_c(\eta)=P_\eta(S_n>c).
\]
Then
\[
\frac{d}{d\eta}\beta_c(\eta)
=
\operatorname{Cov}_\eta(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\},S_n).
\]
Since \(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\}\) is an increasing function of \(S_n\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\eta(\mathbf 1\{S_n>c\},S_n)\ge 0.
\]
Therefore \(\beta_c(\eta)\) is nondecreasing in \(\eta\). Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing in \(\theta\), we also have
\[
P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)\le P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha
\]
for every \(\theta\le \theta_0\). Hence \(\varphi_\alpha\) has size \(\alpha\).

Now fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). By part (d), \(\varphi_\alpha\) is the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test for
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1.
\]
If \(\psi\) is any test with
\[
\sup_{\theta\le \theta_0}E_\theta[\psi]\le \alpha,
\]
then in particular
\[
E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le \alpha.
\]
Therefore, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma,
\[
E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\le E_{\theta_1}[\varphi_\alpha].
\]

Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, \(\varphi_\alpha\) maximizes power simultaneously for every \(\theta>\theta_0\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}
\text{ is UMP level } \alpha.
}
\]

This is the Karlin–Rubin monotone likelihood ratio theorem in this one-parameter exponential family.

---

## (f) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\neq \theta_0\)

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space. Then there exist \(\theta_-<\theta_0<\theta_+\).

We show that, for \(0<\alpha<1\), a nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test does not exist.

For the right-sided simple alternative \(\theta_+>\theta_0\), by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\varphi_+=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\},
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_+)=\alpha.
\]

For the left-sided simple alternative \(\theta_-<\theta_0\), the likelihood ratio
\[
\frac{L(\theta_-)}{L(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0))S_n-n[B(\theta_-)-B(\theta_0)]\right\}
\]
is decreasing in \(S_n\), because \(\eta(\theta_-)<\eta(\theta_0)\). Hence the unique MP level-\(\alpha\) test is
\[
\varphi_-=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\},
\]
where
\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_-)=\alpha.
\]

If a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\varphi\) for the two-sided alternative existed, then it would have to be MP against both \(\theta_+\) and \(\theta_-\). By uniqueness in the Neyman–Pearson lemma, we would need
\[
\varphi=\varphi_+\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
and
\[
\varphi=\varphi_-\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Therefore \(\varphi_+=\varphi_-\) \(P_{\theta_0}\)-a.s.

But this is impossible. The rejection region of \(\varphi_+\) is an upper tail, while the rejection region of \(\varphi_-\) is a lower tail. Since \(S_n\) is continuous and \(0<\alpha<1\), these two regions cannot agree up to a null set.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\text{there is no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test for }
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\text{ vs. }
H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0.
}
\]

A UMP unbiased two-sided test may exist in such exponential families, but a UMP test among all level-\(\alpha\) tests generally does not.
